title: Variations in Soil Microbiome Assembly Determine Hatching Induction of the Carrot Cyst Nematode Heterodera carotae
content:
We evaluated the impact of three soil microbiota, selected by leek, turnip, and barley, on the hatching induction of the cyst nematode Heterodera carotae after carrot root exudate supply. Our results demonstrated that rotation crops can promote the abundance of promising candidate fungal species modulating the hatching induction success.

ABSTRACT
Plants shape their microbiota through root exudation to resist environmental constraints. These plant's exuded metabolites also serve as hatching signals for cyst nematodes, a major crop pest, to trigger their parasitic cycle. The “suicide hatching” strategy takes advantage of these exudates as a decoy, inducing hatching of juveniles in the absence of the host plant. We questioned here the effect of the soil microbiota on the suicide hatching induction. We used the carrot cyst nematode (Heterodera carotae, Jones) and evaluated the impact of three rotation crops (leek, turnip, and barley) and their associated fungal and bacterial communities on the hatching efficacy of carrot exudates in two types of soil. Our results indicated that hatching induction is lower when leek was previously cultivated. By analysing the covariation between hatching and microbiota composition, we identified fungal ASVs, notably Fusarium equiseti, whose abundances correlate significantly with nematode hatching. We validated that diacetoxyscirpenol, a compound produced by this species, significantly reduces nematode hatching induction. Our results demonstrated that rotation crops modulate the composition of the soil microbiome and can promote the abundance of fungi modulating the suicide hatching success. These results provide insights into plant‐microbiota‐nematode interactions for optimizing pest biocontrol strategies.

title: Faecal Bacteria Are Governed by Distinct Assembly Processes Within the Bacterioplankton of an Urban Stream Network
content:
Human faecal bacteria occurred throughout an urban stream network, where environmental selection shaped both faecal and non‐faecal bacterioplankton, but only non‐faecal taxa were dispersal‐limited. Faecal taxa behaved as an external inoculum filtered downstream, with selection tracking surrounding vegetation cover, highlighting input reduction and catchment vegetation as management levers.

ABSTRACT
The ecological fate of human faecal bacteria entering hydrological networks remains poorly understood. We investigated bacterioplankton assembly across an urbanized stream network in the Buenos Aires Metropolitan Area (Argentina), distinguishing faecal from non‐faecal taxa by cross‐referencing 192 human gut microbiome samples from three South American countries; independent source tracking confirmed a predominantly human origin. Faecal taxa occurred throughout the watershed, but their abundance was not significantly associated with Escherichia coli (Spearman's ρ = 0.25; p > 0.05), regardless of the assembly process governing them. Homogeneous selection was the most frequent assembly outcome in both faecal and non‐faecal fractions, yet dispersal limitation separated them sharply: 38.2% of non‐faecal site pairs versus 1.8% of faecal ones. Accordingly, compositional similarity declined with hydrological distance in the non‐faecal fraction but not in the faecal one, where selection was strongest between sites of similar non‐vegetated surface cover. Nestedness contributed far more to faecal than non‐faecal dissimilarity (42.7% vs. 4.3%), consistent with an external inoculum progressively filtered along the network. Faecal and non‐faecal bacterioplankton are therefore shaped by different ecological processes, which single‐indicator monitoring cannot capture. Reducing sanitary inputs, while necessary, should be complemented by strategies enhancing the environmental filtering capacity of urban stream habitats.

title: Dynamics of Antimicrobial Resistant Bacteria in Water Environments: Risks via Surface Waters and Combating Strategies
content:
Discharges from clinical, animal farm, abattoir, and industrial settings into municipal sewers where complex interactions among microorganisms trigger the evolution of ARGs pollutes freshwater sources. Water treatment plants reduce contaminants, but fail to remove them completely. Hence, some ARB escape and enter surface waters used for drinking, recreation, and irrigation. Environmental factors, accompanied by anthropogenic accumulation of antibiotic residues, further drive ARGs dissemination. Advanced treatment plants, constructed wetlands, aquatic macrophyte (like, water hyacinths), microalgae, and phage‐based approaches are effective strategies for managing ARB in surface water systems.

ABSTRACT
Water sustains all living systems, maintaining human, animal, and environmental health. However, as open systems, surface waters are highly exposed to microbial and chemical pollutants, including antimicrobials. These contaminants exert selective pressure on densely packed bacterial genomes and drive mutations leading to adaptation. This review explores the dynamics and key drivers underlying the emergence and persistence of antibiotic‐resistant bacteria (ARB) in aquatic environments. It delineates both classical and novel horizontal gene transfer (HGT) mechanisms, ranging from conjugation, transduction, and transformation to outer membrane vesicles, gene transfer agents, and intercellular nanotubes. These mechanisms promote the evolution, distribution, and stable persistence of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in aquatic systems, including freshwater sources. Furthermore, the review outlines surface water contaminants and their biomagnification risks in the environment and through the consumption of food from freshwater food webs, drinking water, and animal products. Finally, the review discusses potential mitigation strategies, highlighting advanced treatment technologies, constructed wetlands, and biocontrol approaches using aquatic macrophytes (e.g., water hyacinth), microalgae, and phage‐based remediation, while addressing concerns regarding safety, applicability, and scalability. Stewardship programs aligned with One Health frameworks remain vital to mitigating these global risks.

title: Microbially‐Induced Corrosion of Cobalt by Pseudomonas chlororaphis subspecies aureofaciens Is Driven by the Complex Interplay Between Abiotic and Biotic Processes That Control Cobalt Solubility
content:
Cobalt undergoes microbially‐induced corrosion by the bacterium Pseudomonas chlororaphis subspecies aureofaciens. The reaction is initiated by oxygen or redox‐active metabolites that generate cobalt ions that interact with the cell. Corrosion is subsequently driven by unidentified cell‐derived ligands that keep cobalt in solution and inhibit the formation of a passivation layer comprised of cobalt phosphate precipitates.

ABSTRACT
Microbially‐induced corrosion (MIC) driven by redox‐active metabolites has been well studied for iron‐bearing infrastructure, but whether such pathways solubilise economically critical cobalt is poorly understood. This study uses the model bacterium Pseudomonas chlororaphis subspecies aureofaciens to test if redox‐active phenazines corrode elemental cobalt. Mutants incapable of phenazine production corroded as much cobalt as wild‐type cells after one‐week incubations with Co(0) wires, and phenazines alone did not induce corrosion. Anoxic corrosion assays with cell‐free spent medium showed that phenazines can maintain Co(0) oxidation in the absence of oxidants like oxygen, but that oxygen and live cells strongly favour corrosion. Constraining metabolic pathways contributing to corrosion by creating a ∆phz∆hcn mutant led to twice as much cobalt being solubilised compared to the wild type due to metabolic rerouting that could affect the production of putative metallophores. Geochemical and electrochemical analyses suggested these metal‐binding metabolites keep cobalt in solution and prevent the formation of a passivation layer that inhibits MIC. This study shows that complex interactions between abiotic and biotic pathways that control the solubility and bioavailability of cobalt govern MIC. Understanding these mechanisms is critical to mitigating concerns related to MIC damaging infrastructure and optimising sustainable cobalt recovery strategies for solid waste.

title: Oxidative signaling thresholds shape vulnerability in the central and peripheral nervous systems
content:
by Shuji Wakatsuki, Toshiyuki Araki

Neurodegeneration is frequently associated with oxidative stress, yet the mechanisms that convert reactive oxygen species (ROS) into irreversible degenerative signals remain incompletely understood. Neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems often differ in their responses to injury, but these differences cannot be reduced to a simple contrast between weak and strong antioxidant capacity. This Essay proposes that neuronal vulnerability is shaped by multilayered signaling thresholds comprising ROS production, antioxidant and thiol buffering, redox-sensitive signal detection, molecular gating, and commitment to degeneration, survival, or repair. This framework may help explain selective neuronal vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases and identify intervention points downstream of global ROS suppression.

title: Correction: Cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (CIRBP) adjusts clock-gene expression and REM-sleep recovery following sleep deprivation
Declining Surface Solar Radiation Resources in Polar Regions Under Global Warming
content:
Abstract
Surface solar radiation is a key component of the polar energy budget and solar energy resource availability, but biases in climate models limit confidence in future projections. We developed a U‐Net deep learning framework to correct surface solar radiation from 12 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 models using the European Centre for Medium‐Range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis v5 as reference. The correction reduced mean biases by up to 91% and markedly reduced inter‐model spread. Corrected projections under four Shared Socioeconomic Pathways show persistent declines in surface solar radiation and surface solar radiation resources across both polar regions throughout the twenty‐first century, with larger decreases under higher emissions. The Arctic exhibits substantially stronger declines than Antarctica, especially over Greenland and Arctic coastal regions. These results suggest that continued warming will reduce polar surface solar radiation resources and that the Arctic radiation environment is particularly sensitive to greenhouse‐gas forcing.

title: Probing Atmospheric Gravity‐Wave‐Relevant Representations in a Weather Foundation Model via Multi‐Method Fine‐Tuning
content:
Abstract
Weather foundation models pretrained on reanalysis data may encode subgrid‐scale physics beyond their forecasting objectives. Using Aurora, we probe this with a multi‐method fine‐tuning framework: agreement across structurally different adaptation strategies signals shared backbone information, while a matched randomly initialized control isolates pretraining's contribution. We evaluate six methods (0.5%–100% of trainable parameters) for predicting ERA5‐resolved, T21‐filtered gravity‐wave momentum fluxes (313–1,820 km). Evidence for a pretraining benefit is strongest for the zonal flux u′w′ ${u}^{\prime }{w}^{\prime }$: several parameter‐efficient methods outperform random initialization, most clearly FISH + TADP (38.9% vs. 41.6% normalized error, p $p$ = 0.007). The meridional flux v′w′ ${v}^{\prime }{w}^{\prime }$ remains hard for all methods (NRMSE 60%–80%). The benefit is level‐dependent: 11–14 percentage points at 200–300 hPa but only 0.2 at 50 hPa. Approximately 1% of parameters recover part of full‐fine‐tuning skill (38.9% vs. 31.8%), indicating regularization by the frozen backbone.

title: Cloud Controlling Factor Analysis Reveals E3SMv3 Structural Bias and Mean State Controls on Stratocumulus Radiative Sensitivity
content:
Abstract
We investigate marine stratocumulus cloud radiative sensitivity to meteorological and aerosol controlling factors in a perturbed parameter ensemble of the Energy Exascale Earth System Model version 3 (E3SMv3). The ensemble perturbs 25 cloud, convection, and aerosol parameters, spanning diverse cloud behavior. The default simulation and many ensemble members capture observed responses to most controlling factors, but not to surface temperature advection, revealing a structural deficiency in processes linking stratocumulus to advection. Many members also overestimate cloud fraction and radiative responses to inversion strength, free‐tropospheric humidity, and sulfate aerosol optical depth. Differences in mean cloud optical depth substantially modify the radiative impact of similar cloud fraction changes, showing that the mean cloud state strongly regulates stratocumulus radiative sensitivity. Across the ensemble, conversion of cloud water to rain controls mean optical depth, identifying autoconversion as a key microphysical control on stratocumulus radiative sensitivity.

title: Efficient ensemble estimation using an MCMC sampler:  a reconstruction of the Mediterranean low-frequency  variability combining observed and simulated sea level
content:
Efficient ensemble estimation using an MCMC sampler: a reconstruction of the Mediterranean low-frequency variability combining observed and simulated sea level
Jean-Michel Brankart, Damien Héron, Lisa Weiss, Thierry Penduff, and Pierre Brasseur
Ocean Sci., 22, 3207–3224, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3207-2026, 2026

title: Survival-associated cellular communication networks in human solid cancers
content: Single-cell atlases have enabled the prediction of human cell-cell communication (CCC) networks in cancer, but whether predicted communication networks have clinical significance is not well understood. Here, we integrated a pan-solid cancer scRNA-seq atlas comprising 78 cell types from 318,426 quality-controlled cells with bulk RNA-seq and clinical outcome data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) to develop Single-cell-based Kaplan-Meier Analysis Network (SKyNet). SKyNet prioritizes ligand-receptor interactions associated with overall survival across 11 human solid cancers, predicting unique interactions not inferred by previous CCC algorithms. In pancreatic adenocarcinoma, SKyNet-predicted endothelial-pericyte interactions were associated with poor outcomes that were validated by independent spatial transcriptomics and survival cohorts. In lung adenocarcinoma, lymphatic endothelial cell interactions consisting of collagen-integrin pairs were associated with poorer survival outcomes. In kidney renal clear cell carcinoma and kidney renal papillary cell carcinoma, fibroblast communication networks displayed disparate survival associations, with the DSC2-DSG2 axis associated with better survival outcomes. Thus, SKyNet provides a hypothesis-generating framework for cell type-specific communication pathways associated with patient outcomes.

title: Scalable proteomics with multiDIA resolves proteoforms in neurodegenerative disease
content: Deep proteome characterization has traditionally required multidimensional chromatographic fractionation, long acquisition times and large sample amounts, thus limiting scalability. Here, we introduce multiDIA, which combines independent digestions with multiple proteases and data-independent acquisition (DIA) to increase sequence coverage without extensive chromatographic fractionation. By generating complementary and overlapping peptide representations of proteins, multiDIA identifies about 270,000 distinct peptides per sample, including 3,649 phosphosites. This is more than twice the coverage of unfractionated workflows and exceeds the coverage of multidimensional fractionation workflows that use 10-fold more material and time. We demonstrate the approach in Parkinson's disease (PD) brain samples, showing that multiDIA substantially expands sequence coverage while retaining the sensitivity, reproducibility, and scalability of DIA. This enabled the identification of disease-associated proteoform changes undetectable by single-protease DIA and the quantification of many disease-relevant post-translational modifications. MultiDIA thus enables deep, high-confidence proteome characterization from limited sample quantities without the throughput and sensitivity constraints of multidimensional fractionation.

title: Genome-scale metabolic models for a synthetic soil microbial community as a path for understanding community functioning
content: Microbial communities drive essential ecosystem processes, yet community-level behavior often deviates from predictions based on single-species studies. This mismatch reflects the context-dependent nature of nutrient dependencies, metabolic interactions, and resource availability in complex environments. Here, we present a mechanistic, species-resolved framework to dissect metabolism and nutrient exchange in a defined 21-member soil synthetic community spanning five bacterial phyla. For each isolate, we reconstructed and manually curated thermodynamically constrained genome-scale metabolic models, reconciling predictions with growth phenotypes across rich and minimal media. We mapped minimal nutrient requirements, cataloged environment-specific uptake and secretion profiles, and compared metabolic pathways to identify potential competitive and cooperative interactions. Using community-scale metabolomics, we assigned putative producers and consumers for detected metabolites and revealed medium-dependent shifts in niche overlap. This approach exposes metabolic strategies that govern community function and resilience, offering a predictive basis for understanding and manipulating microbiomes. Our findings highlight how species-level metabolic maps can clarify why microbial interventions succeed or fail and guide targeted manipulations in soil ecosystems.

title: Genetic Perturbation Prediction Models Fail Out-of-Distribution: A Rigorous Benchmark and Systematic Evaluation
content: Perturbation prediction models - which forecast transcriptional responses to gene inactivation - are increasingly proposed as in silico surrogates for genome-scale drug discovery screens. Yet, rigorous evaluation of whether these models genuinely generalize beyond their training distribution has been lacking. Existing benchmarks rely predominantly on random train-test splits, obscuring systematic failure modes that only emerge under realistic out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. Here we introduce EL-PERTURB (Extrapolative Learning for PERTURBation Prediction), a benchmarking framework that stress-tests 20 perturbation prediction models spanning six architecture classes on both essential gene and genome-wide Perturb-seq screens, using a novel stratified OOD splitting strategy that partitions train and test sets into functionally distinct regions of transcriptional space. We find that model performance degrades substantially under OOD conditions, and that architectural complexity - including single-cell foundation model embeddings - confers no reliable advantage over well-tuned simpler baselines. EL-PERTURB establishes a rigorous benchmark for perturbation effect prediction across a gradient of generalization difficulty, providing a guide for building models that can genuinely serve as surrogates for wet-lab screening.

title: Benchmarking Microbiome Methods for Improved Metagenomic Sequencing of Lower Respiratory Tract Samples
content: Bronchoalveolar lavage is a common diagnostic strategy used to sample immune cells and microbiota of the lower respiratory tract. Metagenomic sequencing of raw bronchoalveolar lavage fluid reveals a low biomass microbial community often obscured by abundant host DNA. Here, we set out to determine an optimal strategy to robustly purify microbial DNA in excess of human DNA using a combinatorial lysis, host-depletion, DNA extraction approach. We identify strategies that improve metagenomic sequencing success that are commensurate with purification challenges that reduce signal from respiratory microbiota. Finally, we present a general framework to further improve microbial sequencing of lower respiratory tract samples in a robust and reproducible manner.

title: Effects of Alternating Polarity Frequency on the Assembly of Electro-Methanogenic Microbial Communities
content: Electro-methanogenesis can enhance methane production and has attracted extensive interest, but the current strategies for building electro-methanogenic microbial communities suffer from several limitations. Alternating polarity has been shown as a new strategy to build electro-methanogenic communities, but the impact of alternation frequency on community assembly remains to be understood. In this study, the impact was evaluated using bioelectrochemical systems amended with granular activated carbon, and the working-electrode potential was alternated between +0.4 and -0.4 V vs. SHE at six frequencies ranging from 0.5 to 12 days. Among the tested conditions, 4-d alternation led to the best overall performance, producing approximately 250 L/L/kg cumulative biogas, 96% methane content, and a 45% methane yield, while preserving a stable and reproducible community structure. The community contained two Methanobacterium populations, two putatively electroactive Geobacter populations, and one putatively electroactive Pseudomonas population, together with diverse fermentative and syntrophic bacteria. Transcript-based analyses revealed clear frequency- and potential-dependent shifts in the activity of these functional groups. Redundancy analysis associated the Methanobacterium formicicum-related population with cathodic current and methane production, whereas the Geobacter sulfurreducens-related population was linked to anodic current and methane production. Bayesian and local-similarity networks further connected methanogen dynamics with specific electroactive, fermentative, and syntrophic partners. Collectively, these results establish alternating polarity frequency as a critical parameter for building robust communities capable of high-rate, high-quality methane production.

title: Shared genomic features of oral bacterial habitat specialization
content: The oral microbiome exhibits spatial organization, with related bacteria occupying different surfaces despite continual dispersal between habitats. Whether this ecological partitioning is accompanied by genomic functions that recur across evolutionarily divergent lineages remains unclear. Here we compared plaque- and mucosa-associated bacteria representing 47 human microbial taxa, 13 genera and six phyla, using 1,121 reference genome assemblies and habitat-affinity estimates assembled from six oral microbiome abundance summaries. Across 13 genera, a genus-balanced screen of 13,917 nonredundant genomic profiles prioritised 14 exploratory annotations with nominal associations in the same direction before and after adjustment for genome composition with none passing genome-wide family-wise error correction. Proteins carrying recurrent domains belonged to multiple sequence clusters. Closely spaced, divergently oriented HxlR-SnoaL_2 gene pairs occurred in 66 genomes associated with plaque biofilms across four genera, although overall HxlR-SnoaL_2 linkage was not significantly associated with plaque preference. Using source-family-balanced habitat scores, nested cross-validation with entire genera held out supported prediction of habitat preference (macro-average within-genus AUC, 0.821; empirical P = 0.010). Predictive performance was lower after adjustment for genome size, GC content and coding-sequence number (AUC, 0.776; empirical P = 0.059). These findings reveal partial recurrence of habitat-associated genomic annotations amid lineage-dependent protein repertoires and genetic arrangements. They provide a comparative framework for distinguishing broadly shared ecological genomic signatures from alternative, potentially lineage-specific routes to oral habitat specialization.

title: Social anchors: how previous social locations shape current animal movement and habitat selection
content: Memory of past space use is an important factor in habitat selection, but memory of what? The concept of memory captures the geographic spaces that an animal has used in the past. There are, however, competing reasons why animals occupy a given space. Species may occupy space due to particular aspects of their memory. Using integrated step selection analysis, we tested the relative importance of memory: previous use of high forage quality or where social interactions occurred at two temporal scales in caribou (Ranger tarandus). The most important parameter to explain intra-seasonal movement was geographic memory. At the inter-annual scale, caribou more strongly revisited locations with high quality forage and where they had formed dyads with conspecifics. We posit that remembered locations of social fusion can function as social anchors. The effects of memory on movement behaviour depend upon the context, both social and resource-based, and not geographic space alone.

title: The 'false transience' hypothesis: Do we need to reconsider the seed persistence classifications of soil seed bank studies?
content: Background and Aims Seed bank persistence data is typically indirect, inferred from the presence and distribution of seeds in the soil. However, this approach frequently underestimates seed longevity, because dormant and low-abundance seeds can remain undetected. Here, we introduce and test the 'false transience' hypothesis which proposes that a subset of species classified as having transient seeds based on soil seed bank (SSB) studies actually possess the capacity for long-term persistence. Their perceived transience stems from methodological limitations and ecological filters, rather than physiological constraints. We also aimed to assess how the seed mass and seed production of 'false transient' species compare to the full range of tested species. Methods We focused on species considered to have transient seeds based on SSB studies. We conducted a germination experiment with 103 species using dry-stored seeds aged 10-29 years. We then assessed how the seed mass and seed number of germinating species relate to the full range of tested species. Key Results From the 103 tested species, eight species (~8%) germinated. The majority of species germinating after >10 years had large seeds and low seed numbers compared to the full range of species, and all germinating species had seed numbers below the median of the tested species. Conclusions Our results provide partial support for the proposed 'false transience' hypothesis, showing that nearly 10% of supposedly transient species can persist after more than a decade of ex situ storage. Our results also suggest that 'false transients' are frequently large-seeded with low seed production, therefore being more likely to be missed in SSB studies and erroneously classified as transient. We can conclude that relying solely on field SSB data to infer seed persistence can be misleading, suggesting that the widely observed negative relationship between seed size and persistence may also require reconsideration.

title: On Motivating the Choice of Link Function in Binomial Regression Through A Latent Abundance Process
content: Ecologists commonly apply binomial regression to study binary data. Often, the link function in binomial regression is not purposefully chosen, but instead selected on the grounds of interpretation or computation efficiency. However, if the binary response is the result of a latent abundance process, then the link function implies assumptions for this underlying process. The most well-known example of this is the complementary log-log (cloglog) link, which has direct connections with the probability of a positive count under a latent Poisson distribution. If the binary response can be assumed to represent a truncated latent count, the cloglog link can be a better choice than the logit link. On the other hand, counts in ecology are often overdispersed, meaning the assumption of an underlying Poisson abundance process is unrealistic. In this article, we provide a framework for consideration of the link choice in binomial regression, in terms of the latent abundance process that binary responses can represent. Aside from the Poisson case mentioned above, we show that the cloglog link is the right choice if the latent abundance process represents the biomass of individuals, or if the latent abundance process comes from an overdispersed count distribution with a linear mean-variance relationship. For the case where the latent count follows a negative binomial distribution with a quadratic mean-variance relationship, we derive a new generalized complementary log-log (gcloglog) link function, which includes the case of the cloglog link as well as that of the logit link, where the latter implies assuming moderate overdispersion in the form of a geometric distribution. Two simulation studies demonstrate that cloglog and logit link binomial regression can exhibit bias and undercoverage when the latent count is more overdispersed than assumed, while gcloglog link models overcome this issue but in practice require replication in the binomial response for reliable estimation. Two real ecological datasets further illustrate how to use the gcloglog link binomial regression in practice including as a means of sensitivity analysis. We encourage ecologists to give more thought to the choice of link function in binomial regression, based on considering the latent abundance process and its properties.

title: Different paths, same destination: similar benthic nitrogen cycling sustained by distinct biogeochemical mechanisms in artificialized coastal systems
content:
Different paths, same destination: similar benthic nitrogen cycling sustained by distinct biogeochemical mechanisms in artificialized coastal systems
Ludovic Pascal, Éléonore Dansereau-Macias, Carole-Anne Guay, David Didier, Christian Nozais, Luc Sirois, Faten Zouaghi, and Gwénaëlle Chaillou

title: Tuvaijuittuq: The Last Refuge of Multiyear Ice (MYI) Is Becoming Increasingly Open
content:
Abstract
Tuvaijuittuq is currently the largest in a series of Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) in the Canadian Arctic. The remoteness, inaccessibility and paucity of environmental data creates challenges in understanding and establishing conservation management strategies of this unique multiyear ice (MYI)‐dominated region. Here, we apply additive decomposition to monthly time‐series of MYI and first‐year ice (FYI) extents as well as monthly maximum extents of open water, new ice, and young ice in 1999–2020 in six analysis subregions within and directly adjacent to Tuvaijuittuq to analyze trends and seasonality. While increasing openness is uniformly manifested by significant positive trends in open water and its increasing frequency of occurrence, the mechanisms behind these observed changes differ across Tuvaijuittuq. The fjord environments are highly seasonal and their expanding openness is associated with the ongoing strengthening of the seasonal cycle apparent across the Northern Hemisphere. The increasing openness of the Offshore Ellesmere region is attributed to emerging episodic flaw polynyas. Flaw polynya openings north of Ellesmere Island are coinciding with strong and persistent east‐northeasterly winds and dynamic forcing resulting in increased sea ice mobility and observed divergence. We postulate that the observed trends and patterns in increasing openness of Tuvaijuittuq as well as the analysis of seasonality hotspots can provide valuable information for identifying particularly sensitive ecosystems for long‐term monitoring and protection in ice‐dominated MPAs.

title: Contrasting Near‐Inertial Internal Wave Responses to Single Versus Consecutive Typhoons Forcing in the Xisha Islands Waters, South China Sea
content:
Abstract
Mooring observations capture the responses of near‐inertial internal waves (NIWs) to three sequential typhoons (Trami, Yinxing, and Man‐yi) over the Xisha Islands from October to November 2024, using high‐resolution ADCP measurements. Typhoon forcing excites near‐inertial kinetic energy (NIKE) mainly in the 0–100 m layer. Although >90% of NIKE is dissipated within the main thermocline, the remaining energy penetrates below 1,200 m. Nonlinear interactions between DITs and NIWs generate fD1 waves, observed at both the surface and deep layer, indicating their generation is not restricted to the upper ocean. The fD1 waves closely correlate with NIWs and DITs and exhibit pronounced vertical shear, which enhances mixing throughout the water column. Numerical simulations further demonstrate that typhoon‐induced NIWs substantially enhance both near‐inertial potential energy and energy flux. Compared to a single typhoon, consecutive typhoons excite broader near‐inertial spectra and are more favorable for fD1 wave generation. NIKE from a preceding typhoon can superimpose on and resonate with NIKE from subsequent typhoons. NIKE induced by Trami couples with and facilitates downward transmission of NIKE induced by Yinxing and Man‐yi, accompanied by elevated modal structures. Vertically, NIKE shows a layered response: alternating enhancements and weakenings occur in the surface layer (0–200 m), weakening dominates the subsurface (200–600 m), and enhancement prevails below 600 m. As a secondary fluctuation, fD1 wave also undergoes modulation, with enhancement throughout the water column, further promoting mixing. These findings reveal the collective role of consecutive typhoons in modulating NIW dynamics and promoting deep‐ocean mixing.

title: Coastal Freshwater Fate Following Hurricane Harvey
content:
Abstract
Hurricane Harvey made landfall on 25 August 2017 on the Texas coast and produced nearly 162 km3 of freshwater from precipitation on land and sea from 25 August to 1 September. Hydrographic data collected on the Texas continental shelf before and after the passage of Hurricane Harvey (2017) show that by 21 September 2017 (23 days following the storm) nearly 67 km3 of freshwater had altered the coastal ocean hydrography and produced a freshwater coastal plume that stretched more than 200 miles (300 km) from Galveston Bay to South Padre Island, TX. The freshwater volume estimate accounts for roughly 92% of the volume expected to be on the shelf after adjusting for evaporation to the atmosphere and accounting for freshwater that remained on shore in terrestrial containment structures. Terrestrial river gauges account for 20 km3 of the roughly 52 km3 of freshwater water that entered the Gulf of Mexico from land, indicating that the majority (∼60%) of freshwater entered through non‐gauged locations that include over roads, low‐lying land and shallow estuaries. Our findings have challenging implications for prediction modeling of storm impact, surge dynamics, and coastal resource management, which largely rely on gauged station data to monitor discharge, surge, and sea level.

title: The Canadian Arctic as a Source of Trace Metals and Nutrients to the Atlantic Ocean: Fluxes Through Nares Strait, Lancaster Sound, Jones Sound, and Davis Strait
content:
Abstract
The Canadian Arctic Archipelago (CAA) is a shallow conduit conveying Pacific‐ and Atlantic‐derived waters to Baffin Bay via Lancaster Sound, Jones Sound, and Nares Strait. At the southern edge of Baffin Bay, Davis Strait is a key gateway for exchange of Arctic modified water masses with the Labrador Sea and Atlantic Ocean. We estimated trace metal and macronutrient fluxes through major water transport pathways by sampling of these exchange points in 2019, 2021, 2022, and 2024 for iron (Fe), manganese (Mn), cobalt (Co), nickel (Ni), copper (Cu), zinc (Zn), cadmium (Cd), lead (Pb), vanadium (V), barium (Ba), nitrate (NO3), phosphate (PO4), and silicic acid (Si(OH)4). Ultimately, the Arctic waters which have transited the CAA are a source of Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Cd, Pb, Ba, V, and the macronutrients to the Atlantic, while there is no net flux of Fe and Mn across Davis Strait. We propose that rapid warming in the Arctic due to ongoing climate change, and the more frequent failure of the Kane Basin ice arch in Nares Strait will increase the southward flux of Co, Ni, Cu and Cd, but diminish the flux of Mn and Fe. Our results suggest potential changes to micro‐ and macronutrient availability in highly productive regions of the Arctic and in source waters feeding into the North Atlantic.

title: Genome‐Wide Analyses Reveal Spatially Structured Genetic Diversity in Indian Rice Shaped by Ancestry, Geography and Environment
content:
ABSTRACT
India is a major centre of rice diversity, where long‐term cultivation across contrasting environments has generated substantial genomic and phenotypic variation. We analysed genome‐wide SNP variation in 313 Indian rice accessions to resolve ancestry structure, regional diversity, spatial genetic processes, environmental associations and haplotype variation at key domestication and adaptation genes. Population structure analyses resolved eight ancestry groups corresponding to indica, aus, aromatic and japonica lineages. Ancestry explained substantially more genomic differentiation than biogeographic regionalization, while there is extensive historical connectivity among lineages and regions. Genetic diversity considerably varied across biogeographic zones. After balanced resampling, the Himalayan region showed the highest standardized allelic diversity and private‐allele richness, whereas the North‐East region retained high observed heterozygosity and broad ancestry representation. Isolation‐by‐distance was weak overall but strongly lineage‐ and region‐dependent. Spatial principal component analysis identified significant ancestry‐independent broad‐scale genetic gradients, demonstrating geography‐influenced structure beyond lineage composition. Redundancy analysis detected significant genome–environment associations (F = 3.07, p = 0.001), with climate explaining more independent genomic variation (2.7%) than soil (0.9%). District‐level tribal population proportion showed only a weak negative association with individual heterozygosity (Spearman ρ = −0.155, p = 0.006), although PTP classes exhibited low‐to‐moderate genetic differentiation. Haplotype analysis revealed strong locus‐specific ancestry and geographic structuring at sd1, Wx, GS3 and DRO1. Together, the results show that Indian rice diversity is a reticulate genomic mosaic shaped by ancestry, geography, historical gene flow and environmental heterogeneity. This study provides a landscape‐genomic framework for conservation and targeted germplasm utilization in breeding programmes.

title: Turning Red to Green Repeatedly: Ancestral LWS Duplications Drive Convergent Visual Tuning in Teleost Fishes
content:
ABSTRACT
Photopigments, formed by an opsin protein bound to a light‐sensitive chromophore, underlie vertebrate vision. Long‐wavelength–sensitive (LWS) opsins mediate red‐light detection, and most teleosts retain a single functional LWS1. A shorter‐shifted green‐sensitive paralog (LWS2) is found only in a few lineages. By mining teleost genomes and sequencing retinal transcriptomes, we identify elopomorphs as an additional lineage retaining LWS2 (alongside characins and osteoglossomorphs). Surprisingly, we reveal a previously overlooked, shorter‐shifted paralog, LWS3, restricted to gobies (Percomorpha) and arising from an ancestral duplication either in the teleost or in the percomorph ancestor. Structural modelling of twelve LWS opsins reveals convergent evolution at four key amino acid sites (214, 259, 261, 269) in the retinal‐binding pocket, indicating convergent substitutions in human MWS (an old‐world primate‐specific duplicate of the vertebrate LWS1), teleost LWS2, and goby LWS3 relative to red‐sensitive counterparts, consistent with repeated spectral shifts towards greener wavelengths. In several lineages, including characins, mormyrids, gobies, and primates, these shorter‐shifted LWS opsins have at least partially replaced the canonical green‐sensitive RH2‐based visual pigment. Retinal transcriptomes revealed variable lws3 expression across adult gobies, either complementing lws1 in most species, or dominating the visual opsin expression profile as in the sicydiines. In situ hybridisation in the whitebarred goby (Amblygobius phalaena; Valenciennes, 1837) showed that lws1 and lws3 are expressed in separate double‐cone members, analogous to rh2 expression in other fish species. Together, these results show that repeated convergence towards shorter LWS sensitivity in vertebrate evolution involves coordinated changes at the molecular, regulatory, and functional levels, providing a striking example of multilevel sensory adaptation.

title: An integrated human forebrain organoid reveals microglia-mediated CD8<sup>+</sup> T cell recruitment and neuroimmune dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease pathology
content: Genetic evidence implicates immune dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet the neuroimmune mechanisms operating in human tissue remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a modular human forebrain organoid platform that systematically integrates human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia and CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells to reconstitute multicellular AD pathology. This system enables functional interrogation of both innate and adaptive immune components in a human-relevant context. Using this platform, we demonstrate that microglia mediate amyloid-β clearance and neuronal maturation but also drive inflammatory activation and recruit CD8<sup>+</sup> T cells through CCL4/5 signaling via CCR1/5 and CXCR3, establishing a neuroinflammatory feedback loop. Pharmacological targeting of CCR5 or CXCR3 blocks T cell recruitment and modulates autophagy in a microglia-dependent manner. This modular organoid platform provides a versatile tool for dissecting neuron–immune interactions and enables cell-type-specific therapeutic screening in human neuroinflammatory disease models.

title: Multiplexed CRISPRi reveals a transcriptional switch between KLF activators and repressors in the maturing neocortex
content: A critical phase of mammalian brain development takes place after birth. Neurons of the mouse neocortex undergo dramatic changes in their morphology, physiology, and synaptic connections during the first postnatal month, while properties of immature neurons, such as the capacity for robust axon outgrowth, are lost. The genetic and epigenetic programs controlling prenatal development are well studied, but our understanding of the transcriptional mechanisms that regulate postnatal neuronal maturation is comparatively lacking. By integrating chromatin accessibility and gene expression data from two subtypes of neocortical pyramidal neurons in the neonatal and maturing brain, we predicted a role for the Krüppel-like factor (KLF) family of transcription factors in the developmental regulation of neonatally expressed genes. Using a multiplexed CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) knockdown strategy, we found that a shift in expression from KLF activators (Klf6, Klf7) to repressors (Klf9, Klf13) during early postnatal development functions as a transcriptional ‘switch’ to first activate, then repress a set of shared targets with cytoskeletal functions including Tubb2b and Dpysl3. We demonstrate that this switch is buffered by redundancy between KLF paralogs, which our multiplexed CRISPRi strategy is equipped to overcome and study. Our results indicate that competition between activators and repressors within the KLF family regulates a conserved component of the postnatal maturation program that may underlie the loss of intrinsic axon growth in maturing neurons. This could facilitate the transition from axon growth to synaptic refinement required to stabilize mature circuits.

title: More Frequent Atmospheric Rivers and Associated Precipitation Extremes Induced by the Baroclinic Annular Mode
content:
Abstract
Atmospheric rivers (ARs) play a crucial role in the global hydrological cycle, yet how the intrinsic midlatitude atmospheric variability modulates their activity on subseasonal timescales remains poorly understood. Here, we show that AR frequency and landfall in both hemispheres vary strongly with the strength and phase of the Baroclinic Annular Mode (BAM). During its positive phase, BAM increases AR occurrence by up to ∼50% and AR‐driven precipitation extremes by up to ∼40% relative to climatology. Stronger and more frequent ARs during the positive phase of the BAM are primarily driven by enhanced potential‐to‐kinetic energy conversion, which favors AR growth and intensification, particularly in the storm‐track regions. This response is consistent with dynamically enhanced poleward moisture transport due to a more baroclinically unstable and stormier environment. The results underscore the importance of BAM‐related intrinsic midlatitude storm‐track variability in modulating global AR activity and its potential to improve extended‐range AR prediction on subseasonal timescales.

title: How Microporosity Shapes Carbonate Hydraulic Behavior: A Digital Rock Physics Perspective
content:
Abstract
Carbonate hydraulic behavior emerges from flow through pore structures spanning resolvable macropores and sub‐resolution microporous regions, yet the effects of microporosity level and heterogeneity remain poorly understood. We develop and validate a CUDA‐accelerated lattice Boltzmann model that unifies pore‐resolved and continuum flow. Simulations show that low‐velocity microporous regions substantially contribute to bulk flow by activating connections between macropores. Across three carbonate samples, permeability increases nonlinearly with microporosity, with reference permeabilities spanning over two orders of magnitude. Moreover, at fixed bulk porosity, amplifying the observed phase‐wise contrast increases permeability, while spatial permutation controls reveal a dominant contribution from the original spatial organization. Three‐dimensional spatial and pressure‐gradient analyses further indicate that high‐microporosity phases preferentially adjacent to macropores become increasingly conductive as heterogeneity increases, reducing local flow resistance. These results show how naturally organized microporosity controls hydraulic behavior and bulk permeability in multiscale geological porous media.

title: Decadal Creep Acceleration on the Northern Japan Trench Driven by Erosion of Heterogeneously Locked Asperities
content:
Abstract
Geodetic and seismic observations before the 2011 Mw 9.0 Tohoku‐oki earthquake indicate decadal‐scale acceleration of aseismic slip along the northern Japan Trench, but the mechanism remains debated. We show that this transient can be explained by creep‐front propagation that progressively erodes heterogeneously locked asperities. We invert GNSS velocity fields from 1998 to 2009 using a mechanically motivated model in which locked regions are confined to historical rupture areas while their effective sizes and process‐zone stressing rates evolve. The models fit both velocity fields and predict slip accelerations consistent with repeating‐earthquake estimates. Inferred asperities occupied about 66% of their corresponding rupture areas in 1998 and about 37% in 2009, indicating substantial expansion of aseismic creep over the decade before rupture. The inferred shrinkage rates are consistent with fracture‐mechanics predictions for plausible coseismic stress drops. These results suggest that megathrust locking can evolve substantially over decadal timescales.

title: Seasonal and Diurnal Variability of Thermospheric Metastable Helium Observed by Multi‐Platform Observations and Numerical Modeling
content:
Abstract
Metastable helium (He∗ ${\text{He}}^{\ast }$) in the thermosphere emits at 1,083 nm and provides a powerful diagnostic of thermospheric composition, solar radiation, and transport. Its detection remains challenging because of its extremely low density and high‐altitude. Here, we present the first multi‐platform study of thermospheric He∗ ${\text{He}}^{\ast }$ variability using a He∗ ${\text{He}}^{\ast }$ density model, ground‐based LiDAR observations over Danzhou, China, and SPHEREx 1,083 nm measurements from May 2025 to April 2026. The three data sets show consistent seasonal variability, with reduced He∗ ${\text{He}}^{\ast }$‐related signals from late spring to midsummer and enhanced values in autumn and winter. Model results associate this pattern with changes in background ground‐state helium reservoir. A representative diurnal case shows the strongest response at 500–700 km, with enhanced values after 04:50 local time. An additional LiDAR‐observed layer above approximately 950 km is not fully captured by the model, highlighting the need for further He∗ ${\text{He}}^{\ast }$ model development. These results provide observational guidance for helium models.

title: Seasonal cycle in surface seawater isotopic composition
content:
Seasonal cycle in surface seawater isotopic composition
Gilles Reverdin, Claire Waelbroeck, Lola Goeme, Antje H. L. Voelker, and Hans Christian Steen-Larsen
Ocean Sci., 22, 3225–3243, https://doi.org/10.5194/os-22-3225-2026, 2026
